mappings.note: Lead sub-question asks which tone Mandela would NOT have used - reading the speaker's stance (LO-2); the second part asks the learner to elaborate on emancipation being more than political, i.e. the extract's theme (LO-1).
Fills the blanks of a sentence quoted from the text (frightened young man, law-abiding attorney, man without a home). Extraction from the prose, LO-1.
A 100-150 word opinion paragraph on colour prejudice in India, with the option of a humorous treatment - opinion, style and tone, which is C-E1.2. It never returns to Mandela's text.
Mandela's redefinition of courage as the triumph over fear is his message, so LO-2. Not LO-1: the point is the idea, not a retrievable detail like a date.
Setting detail (the sandstone amphitheatre). Straight retrieval from the prose, LO-1.

Requires reading Mandela's flame metaphor and naming what it stands for (man's goodness). LO-6 names exactly this - identifying his figurative language - whereas LO-4 is about set expressions and LO-5 about unfamiliar words.
Date of the inauguration - a stated fact, so LO-1.
Retrieval of where the ceremonies were held, extended by a general-knowledge parallel. The assessable half is extraction from the text, LO-1; no opinion is argued, so not C-E1.2.
Explains what 'an autumn day' means in the southern hemisphere - matching an expression in the text to its intended sense, LO-4, rather than an unfamiliar single word (LO-5).
Asks what 'an extraordinary human disaster' and 'glorious human achievement' refer to - the paradigm case of LO-4, matching Mandela's expressions to their intended meaning.
What Mandela thanks the guests for is stated in the speech; extraction, LO-1.
The pledge that no one will oppress another again is Mandela's vision - the writer's message, LO-2, not a retrievable fact.
The generals' salute and the reason their attitude reversed is character-in-context analysis, LO-2; LO-1 would cover only what they did.
Why two anthems were sung calls for the significance of the moment for both communities - context and message, LO-2.
Retrieves Mandela's two descriptions of government at either end of the century. Information extraction, LO-1.
Same idea as the courage MCQ: Mandela's definition is his message about fear, so LO-2.
Whether love or hate is natural is Mandela's claim about human nature - the writer's message, LO-2, not an extractable detail.
Lists the two obligations Mandela names. He spells them out in the text, so this is retrieval (LO-1), not the expression-matching of LO-4.
The weight of the question is the contrast Mandela draws between transitory and basic freedom - his argument, LO-2, rather than a list of boyhood pastimes.
Mandela's claim that the oppressor is a prisoner of hatred is his message, LO-2.
Asks what the leaders' presence signified - the significance of the occasion in context, LO-2, not the headcount that LO-1 would cover.
'The sum of all those African patriots' is an expression whose intended meaning has to be unpacked - LO-4. It is not a figure of the moment (LO-6) but a phrase about his own standing.
'Would you agree' plus 'add your own examples' is evaluative writing (C-E1.2); 'how does Mandela illustrate this' forces the answer to cite the text, which is LO-3.
Traces how Mandela's idea of freedom widened with experience - the writer's developing message, LO-2.
Fill the blanks with noun forms of the given verbs (contribute/contribution, assist/assistance). Word formation is a grammatical convention, C-E1.3, not vocabulary inference in context.
Explains what pluralising proper names ('the Alexanders, the Napoleons') means in this sentence - an expression matched to its intended sense, LO-4.
Choose which of three paraphrases 'earning my keep' carries in the text. That is literally matching an expression to its intended meaning, LO-4, not deducing an unfamiliar word (LO-5).
Prepare notes and a two-minute speech on true liberty - composition in a set format and register, C-E1.2. The text supplies only the topic.
Completes a sentence taken from the text ('I was not born with a hunger to be free ... I was born free'). Extraction from the prose, LO-1.
Fill-in of the phrase 'democratic, non-racial' from the text. Retrieval, LO-1.
Apartheid as the reason for the diplomatic boycott is stated in the chapter; a retrievable cause, so LO-1 rather than an analysis of Mandela's message.
Completes a quoted line of the speech. Extraction, LO-1.
Names what the nation had still to be liberated from (poverty, deprivation, discrimination) - a sub-theme listed in the speech, which LO-1 covers.
Asks what 'the structure they created' refers to - resolving an expression in the text to its intended referent, LO-4, rather than retrieving a new fact.
What started his hunger for freedom - realising it had already been taken - is Mandela's account of his own awakening, LO-2.
'A country's greatest wealth is its people' is Mandela's value claim, so the writer's message (LO-2) rather than a fact to be looked up.
MCQ on what the two anthems signified - the meaning of the gesture in context, LO-2, matching the short-answer version of the same question.
The paradox that oppression produced men of extraordinary courage is a sub-theme the text states outright; LO-1 names sub-themes.
How the hunger for freedom transformed him - character change across the narrative, LO-2.
Mandela's dream for South Africa is his vision for the future, the writer's message (LO-2), consistent with the other 'ideas for the future' item.
